name: Remineralising toothpaste

lead: Remineralising toothpastes aim to restore minerals to early enamel lesions. They use fluoride, nano-hydroxyapatite, calcium phosphate or bioactive glass.
Fluoride has the best evidence; other agents have less.

paras: Calcium, phosphate and fluoride are redeposited into enamel weakened by acid.
Excess fluoride is a concern in formulation research; follow label directions.

studies.title: Caries clinical trial of a remineralising toothpaste in radiation patients.

lead: Remineralising toothpastes are formulated to help redeposit calcium, phosphate or fluoride into demineralised enamel. Active ingredients include fluoride, nano-hydroxyapatite, amorphous calcium phosphate and bioactive glass.[1]

Fluoride has the strongest support, while evidence for bioactive glass and amorphous calcium phosphate is described as insufficient overall.[1] A double-blind trial in head and neck radiation patients compared a specially formulated remineralising toothpaste with a conventional fluoride toothpaste for caries control.[2]

paras: Nano-hydroxyapatite is a synthetic mineral nearly identical to tooth hydroxyapatite and is used to fill microfissures; such toothpastes reached Europe in the early 2000s.[1] Bioactive glass such as 45S5 gives mineral new sites to form.[1] Research on fluoride-containing bioactive glass for toothpaste notes excess fluoride is problematic.[3]
Fluoride is linked to reduced cavities; evidence for other agents is described as insufficient.[1]

A double-blind randomised trial in radiation patients compared a dual-phase remineralising toothpaste with a 1100 ppm fluoride dentifrice.[2] The abstract available to this article does not state results.

timeline.event: Nano-hydroxyapatite toothpaste approved in Japan as anti-decay agent.[1]
